name: Northeast Couloir

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier to the col, then straight up the line
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, cross it and descend east toward the Stehekin side; Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass, 4.9 miles and 1,800 ft from the trailhead including the camp spur.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the yawning glacier, rope up, and follow the glacier southwest to the Magic-Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. Ski parties also reach this cirque from the Cascade Pass side across the Yawning Glacier without dropping to Pelton Basin.

Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir: roughly 2,000 ft winding down the shoulder, a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 at the very top.

Decide your descent before you leave the col. Reversing the couloir is direct but puts you in a sun-exposed funnel; walking off the South Ridge to the Magic-Hurry-up col and Kool-Aid Lake avoids it entirely but lands you on the opposite side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: April to late June or early July as a snow line, but the road is the constraint: Cascade River Road usually does not open to the Cascade Pass trailhead until the end of June, so a spring ascent means a long road walk or ski from the gate, commonly starting at the Eldorado parking area. In practice late June and early July is the sweet spot, when the road opens and the couloir is still full
hazards: Cliff faces on both sides funnel rockfall down the line — the lower section is potentially a bit of a garbage chute
Documented significant sluffing on spring snow, with large natural avalanches reported in the same zone later the same day
An upper couloir sustaining 45-50 degrees and reaching a proper 50 at the top, often a firm crust under a few inches of new snow
A crevassed Yawning Glacier on the approach and a sun-facing couloir below it, which shortens the descent window
Overhead hazard for the full length of the line
A cornice on the summit ridge in spring
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the Magic-Pelton Col at 6,480 ft, the couloir rises directly above you. That is the test: the line starts at the col, without a traverse. If your next move after reaching the col is to bear back west across the head of the glacier, you are heading for the North Face — a rock route on the same mountain from the same col.

So: pickets and front points mean you are in the right place. This is snow, 40-45 degrees low down and 45-50 above, for about 2,000 ft. If you are slinging blocks and climbing class 4 rock, you have traversed onto the North Face.

The shape of the line is the confirmation: consistently steep but wide, with rock faces on both sides that shed into the gut. A narrow slot, or an open face with no walls beside it, is not this feature. Move through the lower section rather than resting in it — those walls are what make it a funnel.

Be aware that more than one northeast-facing line is described on this mountain and it is not fully clear which is which. One is reached from a col on the northwest shoulder, one from a col named Alliteration Col, and one from the Magic-Pelton col — and two of these are sometimes treated as different lines. The col you stand at is what identifies your line, not the couloir seen from below, so record which col you crossed and how high it was.

And the season is a check in itself: this is a snow route. The line can hold rock or snow depending on the year, but if you have arrived to find loose rock rather than a filled line, the couloir is out of condition and it is the same funnel with nothing holding it together.

beta: The Northeast Couloir is the snow alternative to the North Face and shares its entire approach. From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier (which spans roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft), and follow the glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. From there, instead of traversing west to the north face, take the couloir directly to the summit — the published description allows for either rock or snow depending on the year and the season. Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir and describe it as consistently steep but wide, winding about 2,000 ft down Magic Mountain's shoulder, with a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 degrees at the very top. Expect rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on both sides and heavy sluffing once the sun gets on it — the lower section can turn into a chute for falling debris. This is an early-start, frozen-conditions objective.
overview: A snow line on the peak's northeast flank: follow the North Face approach up the Yawning Glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col, then take the couloir directly to the summit on rock or snow. Known to skiers as the Banana Couloir, with a documented 2,000 ft of consistently steep fall-line.

pitch_detail.notes: From Pelton Basin via easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the glacier (roughly 6,200-6,800 ft), then to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft and the foot of the northeast line. Crevassed. Length apportioned within the reported 2,000 ft total.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 1 — Yawning Glacier to the base of the couloir

pitch_detail.notes: Reported as sustained 40-45 degrees. This is the section most exposed to rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on either side; move through it rather than resting in it.
Reported steepening to 45-50 degrees, with a true 50 degrees at the very top and a firm crust under a few inches of soft snow in the top 100-200 ft. Pickets or a screw belay here.
Sourced: the couloir ascends via rock or snow directly to the summit, depending on the year. Watch for a cornice on the summit ridge in spring. Length apportioned to close the reported total.
